90. sources-consulted-per-category-format: A per-category template gives what was searched in each, or a stated reason it was not (references/synthesizer-prompt.md:99-107)
91. confidence-summary: The answer closes with a sentence or two rating confidence by sub-claim, including what could not be resolved (references/synthesizer-prompt.md:111-113)
92. pre-return-self-check: A seven-question revision list covers citations, tier phrasing, contradictions, gaps, the embedded guess, code-as-intent and tone (references/synthesizer-prompt.md:119-127)
93. repo-evidence-inventory: For repository history, look through commits, PR threads, inline markers, decision records, changelogs and ticket ids (references/sources/code-archaeology.md:5-12)
94. tests-as-edge-case-evidence: Test names and assertions are read for the edge cases that drove a change (references/sources/code-archaeology.md:9)
95. co-change-signal: Files altered in the same commits are treated as evidence of relatedness (references/sources/code-archaeology.md:10)
96. source-control-trust-ranking: Repository history is rated the most trustworthy and complete source because of its direct tie to the code (references/sources/code-archaeology.md:14)
97. rename-following-history: Use `git log --follow` to keep history across renames (references/sources/code-archaeology.md:22)
98. pickaxe-string-search: Use `git log -S` to find commits that added or removed an exact string (references/sources/code-archaeology.md:25)
99. regex-diff-search: Use `git log -G` to find commits whose diffs match a pattern (references/sources/code-archaeology.md:28)
100. commit-diff-inspection: Use `git show` to view one commit in full (references/sources/code-archaeology.md:34)
101. commit-range-history: Use a two-point `git log -p` to see the changes to a file between revisions (references/sources/code-archaeology.md:37)
102. decision-record-search: Search Markdown files for architecture-decision records (references/sources/code-archaeology.md:44)
103. marker-comment-scan: Search the target file with surrounding context for TODO-style markers (references/sources/code-archaeology.md:47)
104. related-test-search: Search test files for the target symbol (references/sources/code-archaeology.md:50)
105. warehouse-source-inventory: The warehouse playbook lists product events, usage and billing events, experiment data, system tables and pipeline lineage as places to look (references/sources/databricks.md:7-11)
106. unqueryable-notebooks-as-gap: A rationale suspected to live in Databricks notebooks is reported as a gap, since the SQL tool cannot see them (references/sources/databricks.md:12)
107. poll-long-query-handle: When the Databricks SQL tool returns a statement id, poll for the result without re-running the query (references/sources/databricks.md:16)
108. probe-schema-before-query: Confirm table and column names with listing and describe statements, and never report from an unverified table (references/sources/databricks.md:18-23)
109. time-bound-warehouse-queries: Every query filters to a window around the ship date, usually about thirty days each side and wider only with strong reason (references/sources/databricks.md:25)
110. prefer-typed-models-over-raw: Query the deduplicated typed dbt models, dropping to raw events only when no model exists or refresh lag matters (references/sources/databricks.md:27)
111. dbt-model-column-conventions: A reference lists the standard columns, property naming and client-context fields to save a describe round-trip (references/sources/databricks.md:29-33)
112. usage-trajectory-pattern: Plot daily event counts around the merge, reading a sudden rise as launch and a decay as deprecation (references/sources/databricks.md:39)
113. threshold-origin-distribution: Compare the pre-PR median, p99 and maximum of a property with a guard's constant to see if the number came from data (references/sources/databricks.md:40)
114. experiment-exposure-lookup: Find the exposure table, then pull counts by variant for the flag near the PR date (references/sources/databricks.md:41)
115. query-history-evidence: For data moves or performance rewrites, filter past executed queries to a tight window and rank by duration or bytes read (references/sources/databricks.md:42)
116. lineage-lead-handback: A dbt model's rationale in git is handed to the source-control investigator instead of being pursued (references/sources/databricks.md:43)
117. error-count-drop-signal: A fall in an error-classifying event after a defensive PR counts as evidence that it resolved that class (references/sources/databricks.md:49)
118. flag-decision-row-signal: An exposure row showing a shipped or concluded decision for the target's flag around ship date counts as good evidence (references/sources/databricks.md:50)
119. instrumentation-does-not-prove-cause: Logging of an event shows interest only, so pair it with a commit or PR citation before claiming causation (references/sources/databricks.md:54)
120. silent-instrumentation-check: Before reading a volume jump as a launch, check for PRs that merely began logging in that window (references/sources/databricks.md:55)
121. schema-drift-awareness: A property on today's model may be missing from older data, or be found only in the raw JSON (references/sources/databricks.md:56)
122. refresh-lag-fallback: For very recent events, query the raw table and deduplicate by id because the models update on a schedule (references/sources/databricks.md:57)
123. retention-cliff-is-gap: A window older than the data's retention or the model's creation is reported as a gap so that it is not read as no activity (references/sources/databricks.md:59)
124. warehouse-finding-record: Each result records type, table, exact query, window, ship-date correlation and strength as direct, circumstantial or weak (references/sources/databricks.md:65-70)
125. numeric-summary-no-raw-rows: Report compact counts, percentiles and first and last timestamps, without dumping rows (references/sources/databricks.md:68)
126. telemetry-artifact-inventory: Look through metrics, monitors, dashboards, traces, logs, incidents and notebooks, where a metric's or monitor's mere existence shows concern (references/sources/datadog.md:7-13)
127. owning-service-first: Begin by finding the responsible services and their dependencies (references/sources/datadog.md:19-24)
128. dashboards-and-monitors-before-raw-data: Check curated views next and note their thresholds, which often explain a clamped value (references/sources/datadog.md:26-33)
129. metric-timeline-correlation: Compare a metric's trajectory with the change date as supporting evidence (references/sources/datadog.md:35-43)
130. narrow-time-bounded-logs: Use log pattern search on symbols or error text within a window around the change, aggregating only for counts (references/sources/datadog.md:45-52)
131. span-and-trace-inspection: Use span statistics and specific traces for timeout, retry, slow-path and cross-service questions (references/sources/datadog.md:54-62)
132. incident-search-for-defensive-code: For defensive targets, search incidents around the time the code was added (references/sources/datadog.md:64-71)
133. monitor-matches-constraint-signal: A monitor whose condition mirrors the code's limit counts as good evidence (references/sources/datadog.md:75)
134. author-dashboard-signal: A dashboard by the target's author whose widgets track what the code guards counts as good evidence (references/sources/datadog.md:76)
135. spike-then-stable-signal: A production spike just before merge followed by stable values counts as good evidence (references/sources/datadog.md:77)
136. incident-reference-signal: An incident naming the code, its symbols or its error strings counts as good evidence (references/sources/datadog.md:78)
137. preceding-log-pattern-signal: A pre-change log pattern the guard would prevent counts as good evidence (references/sources/datadog.md:79)
138. correlation-needs-neighbor-check: A before-and-after shift is only suggestive, so inspect other PRs landing in the same window (references/sources/datadog.md:83)
139. chart-framing-caution: A chart shows what its creator cared about and does not explain a particular line of code (references/sources/datadog.md:84)
140. vanished-telemetry-is-gap: Data missing for the relevant window because of renames, deletion or short retention counts as a gap and not a null result (references/sources/datadog.md:85)
141. aggressive-log-narrowing: Limit log lookups with service, tag and date filters, and aggregate in place of raw dumps (references/sources/datadog.md:86)
142. measured-not-caused: A metric proves interest only, so check it against commit and PR dates (references/sources/datadog.md:87)
143. telemetry-finding-record: Each item records type, name, identifier, owner, dates, the bearing condition or query, and how strong the connection is (references/sources/datadog.md:92-97)
144. incident-ticket-labels: Look for tracker items labelled as incident, severity, postmortem action or reliability (references/sources/incident-postmortem.md:3)
145. incident-channel-date-search: Search severity and incident channels near the date the target first appeared (references/sources/incident-postmortem.md:4)
146. incident-commit-message-signals: Treat commit subjects about incidents, added guards, or a revert followed by a re-application as strong signals (references/sources/incident-postmortem.md:5)
147. ticket-evidence-inventory: Tracker evidence includes descriptions, attached project docs, hierarchy, comments, labels, status updates and linked PRs (references/sources/linear.md:5-11)
148. linked-tickets-first: Fetch ticket ids named in seed commits or PRs before anything else, including their comments (references/sources/linear.md:19)
149. multi-phrasing-ticket-search: Search by feature name, symbol and business term using several wordings (references/sources/linear.md:20)
150. walk-up-to-parent-ticket: From a tactical sub-issue, fetch the parent, which often carries the motive (references/sources/linear.md:21)
151. read-project-documents: Check documents attached to an issue's project, where specs often sit (references/sources/linear.md:22)
152. labels-and-milestones-as-motive: Read labels for the type of motive and milestones for deadlines (references/sources/linear.md:23)
153. ticket-good-evidence-shapes: Good evidence includes a stated business problem, a recorded decision comment, an initiative-named parent, an attached spec and motive-bearing labels (references/sources/linear.md:27-31)
154. ticket-scope-drift-check: Read a ticket's whole history because it may have reopened with a different scope (references/sources/linear.md:35)
155. boilerplate-rationale-discount: Generic text in a mandatory rationale field is not accepted as a real answer (references/sources/linear.md:36)
156. stale-ticket-date-check: Compare ticket dates with the code's ship date, since old plans change (references/sources/linear.md:37)
157. follow-duplicate-chains: Trace closed-as-duplicate links to the canonical ticket (references/sources/linear.md:38)
158. inaccessible-item-as-gap: Report tickets you cannot access as a gap and do not guess at their contents (references/sources/linear.md:39)
159. ticket-finding-record: Each ticket records id, title, exact motive quote, labels, parent, project, author, dates and link (references/sources/linear.md:44-48)
160. document-evidence-inventory: Long-form evidence includes requirement docs, specs, decision records, meeting notes, team pages, postmortems, runbooks and strategy docs (references/sources/notion.md:5-12)
161. document-keyword-set: Query by feature, symbols, author handles, error or user-facing terms, and time bounds when the ship date is known (references/sources/notion.md:20-25)
162. read-full-page-not-preview: Fetch whole pages, since reasoning often sits mid-document (references/sources/notion.md:26)
163. follow-backlinks-and-subpages: Check child pages and backlinks for alternatives, appendices and implementation notes (references/sources/notion.md:27)
164. query-meeting-note-databases: Query related databases for meeting notes about the decision (references/sources/notion.md:28)
165. author-personal-spaces: Check the PR author's personal notes for earlier exploratory thinking (references/sources/notion.md:29)
166. document-good-evidence-shapes: Good evidence includes a matching problem section, rejected approaches, a postmortem naming the fix, dated decision notes and a filled decision record (references/sources/notion.md:33-37)
167. outdated-doc-cross-check: Compare a spec with the actual PR because specs often predate implementation and go stale (references/sources/notion.md:41)
168. doc-reality-divergence-flag: When a document and the code differ, flag it for the synthesizer to surface (references/sources/notion.md:42)
169. specificity-over-template-fluff: Discount filler in required sections and look for specific content (references/sources/notion.md:43)
170. broad-search-for-unlinked-docs: Use broad keywords because the best document may have no inbound link (references/sources/notion.md:44)
171. pick-final-draft-by-date: Among several documents on a topic, use the finalized or most recently updated one (references/sources/notion.md:45)
172. restricted-page-as-gap: Log a page you cannot open as a gap (references/sources/notion.md:46)
173. document-finding-record: Each document records title, URL, authors, update date, verbatim motive with its location, linked pages and final or draft status (references/sources/notion.md:51-55)
174. orient-org-and-project: When the error-tracker project and organization are unknown, look them up first (references/sources/sentry.md:7-12)
175. error-query-construction: Build searches from handled exception classes, function or class names, checked messages and the file path (references/sources/sentry.md:20)
176. error-lifecycle-against-ship-date: Check first and last seen, affected releases and frequency trend to see if the stop lines up with the change (references/sources/sentry.md:22-29)
177. stack-trace-relevance-check: Open a full event to see if its trace crosses the target and its tags and breadcrumbs match the guarded condition (references/sources/sentry.md:31-37)
178. release-cross-reference: Compare releases near the commit date with the PR's merge date (references/sources/sentry.md:39-45)
179. ai-root-cause-as-hypothesis-only: Use Seer analyses sparingly as inference, with actual events and traces as the primary evidence (references/sources/sentry.md:47-53)
180. error-finding-record: Each issue records id, title, project, seen timestamps, event count with sampling, releases, a verbatim trace excerpt, ship-date correlation, link and author notes (references/sources/sentry.md:58-66)
181. inspect-chat-tool-schema-first: Chat tooling varies, so check which one exists and its schema, and whether it needs authentication, before searching (references/sources/slack.md:5)
182. auth-failure-stop-and-report: If the tool cannot authenticate, stop and report it as unsearchable, inventing no findings (references/sources/slack.md:17)
183. author-bounded-chat-search: Search the PR author's messages around the merge date to shrink the scope (references/sources/slack.md:7)
184. pr-url-chat-search: Search for the PR's link or number (references/sources/slack.md:8)
185. error-string-chat-search: Search for an error string the code handles, which tends to surface incident threads (references/sources/slack.md:9)
186. chat-retention-note: Report the date before which messages appear to have been deleted by retention (references/sources/slack.md:13)
187. private-messages-known-limitation: Accept that decisions in private messages cannot be searched, and treat this as a stated blind spot (references/sources/slack.md:14)
188. casual-remark-not-a-decision: A flippant remark before a commit does not count as a decision, so look for considered discussion (references/sources/slack.md:15)
189. always-fetch-chat-thread: Read the full thread because a lone message can mislead (references/sources/slack.md:16)

### Traits

- `stated-scope-reading` (new): absent; adopt, pending → explain-code; guide ok [U-02]; modification: Into `immaterial-ambiguity-reading`. Limited to immaterial ambiguity; material ambiguity is asked under `AGENTS.md`.; reason: Lands in explain-code, SKILL.md, into `immaterial-ambiguity-reading`. Upstream: SKILL.md:23.
- `role-model-config-line` (new): absent; reject; reason: Model choice goes through the delegation skill and its roster, never a line in a unit (playbook-map §7.1 item 5).
- `rejected-model-swap` (new): absent; reject; reason: Delegation asks the owner when no entry exists (owner-roster); a silent family swap is what it forbids.
- `job-fit-helper-effort` (new): absent; reject; reason: AGENTS.md "use configured models and reasoning effort" holds (configured-model-use).
- `writable-helper-mode` (new): absent; reject; reason: A vendor tool limit, not a rule for us; explain-code stays read-only.
- `brief-only-read-only` (new): absent; reject; reason: The delegation skill holds enforced-read-only; the unit-level rule is our own read-only-explanation.
- `question-typing` (new): absent; reject; reason: explain-code's branch conditions already pick how, history or decision; a finer type changes no step.
- `code-anchor-first` (new): absent; adopt, pending → explain-code; guide ok [U-01]; reason: Lands in explain-code, references/history.md. Upstream: SKILL.md:27, references/sources/code-archaeology.md:22.
- `pr-discussion-pull` (new): absent; defer; revisit when: the project keeps rationale in pull request threads; reason: This repository keeps rationale in Beads and decision records and has no pull request flow.
- `investigator-brief-assembly` (new): absent; reject; reason: The delegation skill owns briefs (worker-brief-contents); explain-code fixes no investigators.
- `full-coverage-search` (new): absent; reject; reason: The repository has few local sources and local-evidence-sources searches them all; a coverage map across absent sources says nothing here.
- `sources-consulted-line` (new): absent; adopt, pending → explain-code; guide ok [U-05, U-06]; reason: Lands in explain-code, references/history.md. Upstream: SKILL.md:31, 70, 92, references/synthesizer-prompt.md:99-107.
- `evidence-source-discovery` (new): absent; reject; reason: local-evidence-sources names what to search, so discovering source kinds adds nothing here.
- `evidence-category-fanout` (new): absent; adopt, pending → explain-code; guide ok [U-01, U-07]; modification: Into `local-evidence-sources`. Drops the fan-out and its fixed investigators for one pass over the local sources; commit messages are always searched.; reason: Lands in explain-code, references/history.md, into `local-evidence-sources`. Upstream: SKILL.md:49, 60.
- `repo-evidence-inventory` (new): absent; adopt, pending → explain-code; guide ok [U-01]; modification: Into `local-evidence-sources`. Drops pull request threads, which wait on pr-discussion-pull, and ticket ids, which Beads replace; commits, inline markers, decision records, changelogs, tests and co-changed files stay.; reason: Lands in explain-code, references/history.md, into `local-evidence-sources`. Upstream: references/sources/code-archaeology.md:5-12, 44, 47, 50.

Suggested: principle-boundary-discipline · purpose match: codebase-design · flag: suggested differs
Purpose: Upstream sketches types, signatures and module shape through parallel runners and then implements against the result. Our codebase-design is the lens for the same module-interface decisions and gains a sketch branch that stops before code (ruling 5).
Reason: Compared with codebase-design by purpose. Overlap is one trait, depth-as-leverage, against four for principle-boundary-discipline, whose traits units cite and never list. Suggested principle-boundary-discipline by the computed signals only.

### Blind extraction

1. stub-body-design-sketch: Draft types, signatures, classes and module edges using unimplemented bodies and pseudocode before writing real code (SKILL.md:9)
2. phase-todolist-at-start: Open a task list with one item for each of five phases before beginning (SKILL.md:13-19)
3. grounding-gate: Understand each affected system through a full architectural explanation, and do not count naming a file as grounding (SKILL.md:23)
4. rationale-grounding-for-ownership-changes: When a design changes who owns what or how layers divide, also investigate why the existing shape exists so that its reason becomes a constraint (SKILL.md:23)
5. greenfield-grounding-exception: Grounding may be skipped only for true greenfield work with nothing to integrate (SKILL.md:25)
6. multi-model-candidate-competition: Produce candidates through parallel runners on different models, fed the grounding artifacts and synthesized into one design package (SKILL.md:29)
7. runner-model-config-line: Runner models come from a dedicated line in the shared model-config rule, overriding the competition's generic runner line (SKILL.md:31)
8. runner-default-model-pair: Without that line, the runners are `claude-opus-5-5-xhigh` and `grok-4.7-xhigh-fast` (SKILL.md:31)
9. at-least-two-distinct-designs: Require two or more structurally different candidates before synthesis even if the first looks adequate (SKILL.md:33)
10. whole-shape-alternatives: Alternatives must differ in overall shape, and variations inside one shape do not qualify (SKILL.md:33)
11. red-flag-screen-before-synthesis: Check every candidate against a design-flaw list before combining them (SKILL.md:35)
12. agent-contributor-assumption: Judge designs assuming the next editor is an agent that sees only opened files, imitates whatever example is closest and picks the quickest route that compiles (SKILL.md:35)
13. locally-right-is-globally-right: Prefer a design in which an edit that seems correct from one file is correct for the repository (SKILL.md:35)
14. interface-depth-comparison: Rank viable candidates by how much complexity sits behind how small a public surface (SKILL.md:37)
15. rich-interface-over-layers: A capable interface may be preferred because it keeps call chains short by gathering capability in one place (SKILL.md:37)
16. synthesis-decision-recorded: The combination step's decision is written into the rationale (SKILL.md:39)
17. no-checkpoint-by-default: Implementation follows the synthesized design with no human stop (SKILL.md:43)
18. opt-in-signoff-checkpoint: If the invoker explicitly asks, show the synthesized design and wait for approval (SKILL.md:45)
19. scaffold-as-own-commit: The synthesized sketch may be committed separately before implementation (SKILL.md:47)
20. planned-breakage-during-fill-in: Scoped, planned breakage while filling in the sketch is acceptable (SKILL.md:47)
21. pushback-triggers-regrounding: Human objection to the shape, during or after a checkpoint, counts as grounding evidence and forces a return to grounding and sketching before more code (SKILL.md:49)
22. sketch-as-contract: Implementation replaces stubs and pseudocode, and the agreed sketch governs that work (SKILL.md:53)
23. surface-deviations-with-triage: Raise any departure from the sketch and ask if the fault lies with the sketch, an overlooked requirement or an overreaching implementation (SKILL.md:53)
24. scrap-on-persistent-friction: Discard the sketch when implementation repeatedly produces friction it cannot absorb, without patching a wrong design (SKILL.md:57)
25. pattern-not-instance-threshold: The scrap decision rests on recurrence and not on isolated problems, and a few edge cases or complex data do not condemn a design (SKILL.md:59)
26. tell-repeated-workaround: The same workaround form recurring across unrelated code signals a wrong design (SKILL.md:61)
27. tell-special-case-branches: Several unrelated edge cases each needing a special branch signals a wrong design (SKILL.md:62)
28. tell-type-escape-hatches: Types that compile only with loose types, casts or fields that are optional yet always set signal a wrong design (SKILL.md:63)
29. tell-lock-on-unshared-state: Wanting a lock on state the sketch called unshared signals a wrong design (SKILL.md:64)
30. tell-callers-know-internals: Callers needing the abstraction's internal rules signals a wrong design (SKILL.md:65)
31. tell-repeated-deviations: Two or more independent departures of the same form signal a wrong design (SKILL.md:66)
32. scrap-reexplain-what-exists: After scrapping, produce a fresh explanation of what has been built (SKILL.md:72)
33. redesign-with-day-one-assumptions: Redesign as though the newly learned constraints had been known from the beginning (SKILL.md:73)
34. shrink-before-growth: The replacement sketch must first shrink below the old sketch's size, and only then expand (SKILL.md:74)
35. rerun-competition-after-scrap: Return to the candidate competition after scrapping (SKILL.md:75)
36. output-scales-with-change-size: Small changes yield one file of types and signatures, and larger work yields a module map plus type definitions (SKILL.md:79)
37. rationale-ships-with-sketch: A prose rationale accompanies the type sketch as a deliverable (SKILL.md:79)
38. red-flag-means-revise-or-reject: Any hit on the design-flaw list is grounds to rework or drop the shape (references/design-red-flags.md:3)
39. shallow-module-flag: Reject wide interfaces hiding little, judging depth by hidden capability and policy relative to surface size (references/design-red-flags.md:7)
40. deep-module-not-deep-call-chain: Distinguish concentrating capability behind one interface from spreading understanding across layers (references/design-red-flags.md:9)
41. shallow-module-signs: Signs of shallowness are callers coordinating several methods for one operation, options exposing internal stages and an interface that does not spare learning the implementation (references/design-red-flags.md:13-15)
42. information-leakage-flag: Reject designs in which one internal decision appears in several modules and changing it needs coordinated edits (references/design-red-flags.md:19)
43. no-wire-types-in-public-api: Keep transport types, storage layouts, framework values and protocol specifics private, and convert external data to domain types behind the interface (references/design-red-flags.md:21)
44. temporal-decomposition-flag: Reject modules organized by execution order, and group by owned knowledge even when methods run at different times (references/design-red-flags.md:25-27)
45. pass-through-method-flag: Remove same-shape forwarding methods, unless they add policy, adaptation or a distinct abstraction (references/design-red-flags.md:31-33)
46. split-ownership-flag: Each piece of state gets one owner, so that others read it or request changes, and neither duplicate writers nor copies arise (references/design-red-flags.md:37-39)
47. two-ways-flag: Keep a single way to do a task, moving callers off and deleting the others in the same change (references/design-red-flags.md:43-45)
48. importable-internals-flag: Make internals unreachable so that an outside import fails the build (references/design-red-flags.md:49-51)
49. hand-synced-list-flag: Derive duplicate lists from one, or make the build fail when underivable lists disagree (references/design-red-flags.md:55-57)
50. one-page-rationale: The rationale is limited to one page with sentence-case headings and no boilerplate (references/rationale-template.md:3)
51. problem-section-with-constraints: One paragraph states the goal, what makes the shape non-obvious and any grounding constraints such as interop types, unbreakable callers and invariants (references/rationale-template.md:7)
52. usage-first-spec: Write a quickstart and two or three realistic call sites before the types, derive the types from them, and reconcile any divergence toward the usage (references/rationale-template.md:11)
53. shape-section-data-first: Describe the architecture beginning with data structures, then the flow of data through signatures, naming the load-bearing decisions (references/rationale-template.md:15)
54. invariant-validation-and-non-goal-statement: State which invariants live in types, where validation sits and what the system deliberately omits (references/rationale-template.md:15)
55. explicit-interface-depth-judgment: State what the surface hides, what it exposes and why it is no larger than needed (references/rationale-template.md:15)
56. cite-principle-no-restatement: Attach the governing principle to each decision by name without repeating it (references/rationale-template.md:15)
57. synthesis-decision-section: Record the chosen base candidate with its reason, what was grafted from the rest and the reasons for each rejection (references/rationale-template.md:19)
58. accepted-tradeoff-bullets: Each tradeoff is one bullet in an accept-this-in-exchange-for-that form, including choices a later reader might mistake for an oversight (references/rationale-template.md:23)
59. required-alternatives-section: Name at least one concrete losing shape with a one-line reason, judged on interface depth, excluding flavors of one shape and other runners' candidates (references/rationale-template.md:27)
60. forced-answer-phrasing: When constraints allow just one alternative, say explicitly that it was the only viable shape and why (references/rationale-template.md:27)
61. open-questions-phrased-as-questions: Items and risks needing human judgment are posed as questions, so that the reply resolves them (references/rationale-template.md:31)
62. one-sentence-next-step: State in one sentence what gets built first from the sketch (references/rationale-template.md:35)
63. isolated-runner-workspace: Each runner works in its own git worktree or, failing that, a per-runner subdirectory, so that candidates stay independent (references/runner-prompt.md:3)
64. runner-reads-workflow-first: A runner reads the enclosing design workflow in full before starting (references/runner-prompt.md:5)
65. candidate-package-contents: Each runner delivers a type sketch, signatures, a module map and a templated rationale (references/runner-prompt.md:5)
66. discipline-axes-for-base-selection: The orchestrator compares candidates on the listed design disciplines to choose a base (references/runner-prompt.md:7)
67. data-structures-first: Settle core types first and trace each dominant access pattern through them, treating a planned future map, index or cache as proof that the structure is wrong (references/runner-prompt.md:10)
68. pull-complexity-into-callee: Favor a simple interface even when the implementation becomes harder (references/runner-prompt.md:11)
69. per-actor-state-with-read-merge: If two actors might write the same state and the outcome is not harmless, default to separate state merged at read time (references/runner-prompt.md:12)
70. visible-boundaries-in-sketch: Use unimplemented errors, TODO pseudocode and intent-and-invariant doc comments so that data can be traced by reading only types and signatures (references/runner-prompt.md:13)
71. invariant-enforcement-ranking: Prefer hard-to-misuse types over runtime checks, and runtime checks over comments (references/runner-prompt.md:14)
72. validate-at-boundaries-trust-inside: Check data at the edge and rely on types internally (references/runner-prompt.md:15)
73. pure-core-thin-shell: Write business logic as pure functions behind a thin outer layer (references/runner-prompt.md:15)
74. single-source-of-truth: Each invariant has one authoritative home, and the rest is derived and not synchronized (references/runner-prompt.md:16)
75. idempotent-transitions-check: Where applicable, ask what happens on a repeat run or a mid-way crash and make state changes idempotent (references/runner-prompt.md:17)
76. three-file-call-chain-limit: Flatten the hierarchy if following the flow takes more than three files (references/runner-prompt.md:18)
77. no-hedging-across-runners: Each runner produces its model's strongest design, because differences drive the selection and a safe middle defeats the purpose (references/runner-prompt.md:20)

Suggested: html-artifact · purpose match: none · flag: suggested differs
Purpose: Upstream edits text by numbered rules to remove patterns that read as machine-written. Ours has no such unit until prose-pass is built; authoring-for-agents owns agent-facing text only.
Reason: Compared with none: prose-pass, the row target, does not exist yet, and --with takes only an existing skill. Suggested html-artifact by the computed signals only. Blind lines dropped as not traits: `scan-then-rewrite` (Not material: the order of one edit pass, with no gate or output of its own.).

### Blind extraction

1. preserve-meaning-and-tone: Edits keep the original sense and fit the intended tone (SKILL.md:9)
2. stable-rule-numbers: Rule numbers are permanent identifiers that other documents can cite, and deleting a rule leaves its number unused (SKILL.md:13)
3. rule-3-trailing-participle-clauses: Rule 3 deletes, or backs with real sources, tacked-on present-participle phrases that claim significance (SKILL.md:17)
4. rule-5-unnamed-authorities: Rule 5 requires naming the source of any claim credited to unnamed groups, or deleting the claim (SKILL.md:18)
5. rule-7-machine-vocabulary-list: Rule 7 replaces a fixed list of overused elevated words with plain ones (SKILL.md:22)
6. rule-8-inflated-copulas: Rule 8 swaps grand verbs standing in for being or having with those two plain verbs (SKILL.md:23)
7. rule-9-negative-parallelism: Rule 9 removes the two-part construction that denies one thing to promote another, and states the point straight (SKILL.md:24)
8. rule-10-forced-triads: Rule 10 lists as many items as naturally exist and does not force a group of three (SKILL.md:25)
9. rule-11-synonym-cycling: Rule 11 keeps one term for one referent and does not rotate through synonyms (SKILL.md:26)
10. rule-12-false-ranges: Rule 12 replaces a span construction lacking a real scale with a direct list (SKILL.md:27)
11. rule-13-no-em-dashes: Rule 13 bans em dashes and their substitutes, including parentheses, en dashes and hyphens as dashes, leaving only periods and commas to separate thoughts (SKILL.md:31)
12. rule-14-colon-restraint: Rule 14 allows colons before lists or examples and rewrites mid-sentence uses, also removing comparison framing (SKILL.md:32)
13. rule-15-boldface-restraint: Rule 15 stops bolding every proper noun or acronym (SKILL.md:33)
14. rule-16-inline-header-lists: Rule 16 converts bullets whose bold label merely restates the line into prose, while allowing a period-ended label followed by new detail (SKILL.md:34)
15. rule-17-sentence-case-headings: Rule 17 requires sentence case in headings (SKILL.md:35)
16. rule-18-no-decorative-emoji: Rule 18 strips ornamental emoji from headings and bullets (SKILL.md:36)
17. rule-19-straight-quotes: Rule 19 replaces typographic quotation marks with straight ones (SKILL.md:37)
18. rule-20-chatbot-phrases: Rule 20 removes assistant pleasantries, offers of further help and excited discovery lines (SKILL.md:41)
19. rule-22-no-flattery: Rule 22 drops praise and agreement openers, and answers directly (SKILL.md:42)
20. rule-23-filler-phrases: Rule 23 shortens wordy stock phrases and deletes empty importance announcements (SKILL.md:46)
21. rule-24-stacked-hedges: Rule 24 reduces piled-up qualifiers to a single modal (SKILL.md:47)
22. rule-25-generic-conclusions: Rule 25 replaces optimistic sign-offs with specific plans or facts (SKILL.md:48)
23. rule-26-abstract-metaphor-nouns: Rule 26 replaces a listed set of pseudo-technical figurative nouns with their concrete equivalents (SKILL.md:52)
24. rule-27-mechanism-over-feeling: Rule 27 rewrites sentences that convey an impression so that they state a mechanism or number, and cuts any that cannot become an instruction, fact or figure (SKILL.md:56)
25. rule-27-portability-test: Also under rule 27, a sentence that would fit another project's docs without change gets cut (SKILL.md:56)
26. rule-28-one-idea-per-sentence: Rule 28 splits or trims any sentence the reader must reread to parse (SKILL.md:57)
27. rule-29-active-voice: Rule 29 turns passive constructions into ones naming the actor, keeping passive only for an actor nobody knows or cares about (SKILL.md:58)
28. rule-30-adverbs-to-strong-verbs: Rule 30 cuts adverbs, using a stronger verb or the measured figure in their place (SKILL.md:59)
29. rule-31-plain-word-choice: Rule 31 swaps fancier synonyms for common words (SKILL.md:60)
30. rule-32-literal-over-mannered: Rule 32 replaces aphorisms, rhetorical fragments, personified code, figurative verbs and stock framing with literal phrasing (SKILL.md:61)
31. rule-33-no-over-compression: Rule 33 restores articles, verbs and whole sentences and spells out arrows, symbols and abbreviations (SKILL.md:62)
